title-group.article-title: Exploring the global research trends and precise therapeutic indications of colchicine for coronary heart disease: A bibliometric systematic review and meta-analysis

sec.title: Background:
sec.p: Colchicine has garnered significant interest in its potential role in reducing cardiovascular events in coronary heart disease (CHD) patients. Recent studies have shown varying results regarding its efficacy, particularly in stable CHD (SCHD) and acute coronary syndromes (ACS). Additionally, the precise clinical indications and molecular mechanisms of colchicine in the treatment of CHD remain ambiguous. Our study aims to review the current research status of colchicine for CHD, and explore future trends and potential beneficiary populations.

sec.title: Methods:
sec.p: We searched Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases for relevant research findings regarding the application of colchicine for CHD from inception through February 28, 2025. Bibliometric methods were performed to analyze research trends in this field. Meta-analysis was conducted to investigate our primary endpoints of interest, including recurrent myocardial infarction, stroke, revascularization, and cardiovascular death.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: The overall trend of research in colchicine for CHD continued to increase from 2013 onward and peaked in 2021. Research hotspots can be summarized into 4 domains: (1) diseases and drug therapy, (2) molecular mechanisms of colchicine, (3) network pharmacology, and (4) secondary prevention and adverse effect monitoring. In addition, our meta-analysis revealed that colchicine yielded a 20% relative reduction in recurrent myocardial infarction (P < .05), a 46% relative reduction in stroke (P < .05), and a 34% relative reduction in revascularization (P < .05). Subgroup analyses revealed a novel finding that colchicine showed a promising decline in the primary endpoints among SCHD patients, whereas these benefits were absent in ACS patients.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: Considering that the molecular mechanisms of colchicine remain unclear, the global research results suggested that it may be more suitable for SCHD patients with high residual inflammation risk. This finding aligns with the growing body of evidence supporting the role of inflammation in the progression of CHD. However, the inconsistent results in ACS patients highlight the need for large-scale, multicenter trials to better understand the clinical utility of colchicine in different CHD subtypes. Moreover, progress in the exploration of the underlying mechanisms and secondary prevention will confer benefits to CHD patients who receive colchicine therapy.
Keywords: colchicine, coronary heart disease, major adverse cardiovascular events, molecular mechanisms, therapeutic indications
Received 2025 Mar 13; Received 2025 Apr 28; Accepted 2025 May 14; Collection date 2025 May 30.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Coronary heart disease (CHD) remains the first leading cause of death globally, and likewise the major cause of death in China.[1] The high mortality and morbidity rates of CHD are a major global public health problem that needs to be urgently addressed. Nowadays, dual anti-platelet and lipid-lowering therapies are the primary treatment options for CHD. These approaches have prolonged patient survival and improved their quality of life, but some clinical trials revealed that residual inflammatory risk was a strong determinant of recurrent adverse cardiovascular events even after achieving guideline-recommended lipid reductions.[2] Therefore, there is an active pursuit of new complementary avenues to the existing therapeutic strategy for atherosclerotic disease.

In 2017 CANTOS trial (the canakinumab anti-inflammatory thrombosis outcomes study) demonstrated that canakinumab yielded markedly cardiovascular benefits through targeting interleukin-1β, which was the first successful randomized controlled trial with anti-inflammatory treatment for CHD.[3,4] However, this anti-inflammatory agent was associated with a high incidence of fatal infection.[3,4] Further efforts in several clinical studies were then made to confirm that colchicine showed distinctive cardiovascular protection with minimal side effects.[5–9] Subsequently, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved colchicine as an adjunct to low-density lipoprotein cholesterol-lowering therapy for CHD.[1,10] Numerous clinical researchers in different countries have made tremendous progress on the treatment effects of colchicine and the number of related publications has increased dramatically.[4,9] However, the recent results from the CLEAR SYNERGY trial have demonstrated that colchicine did not reduce the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with acute coronary syndromes (ACS). This negative result has reignited debates regarding the clinical utility of colchicine, prompting clinicians to question its efficacy and the potential need for a reevaluation of current guideline recommendations. Furthermore, no recent studies have analyzed the overall trend of this application and the focus of future research. In this study, we employed bibliometric methods to analyze publications on colchicine treatment for CHD from inception to 2025, and mapped the research hotspots and trends. Additionally, we conducted a meta-analysis to summarize the clinical benefits of colchicine and provide direction for future investigations.

sec.title: 2.1. Source of the data and search strategy
sec.p: We sourced all publications for our study from the Web of Science Core Collection database from inception through 2025. Search strategies were set as follows: TS (title/abstract) = ((TS = (Myocardial Ischemia OR Ischemia, Myocardial OR Ischemias, Myocardial OR Myocardial Ischemias OR Ischemic Heart Disease OR Heart Disease, Ischemic OR Disease, Ischemic Heart OR Diseases, Ischemic Heart OR Heart Diseases, Ischemic OR Ischemic Heart Diseases) AND TS = (colchicine)) AND LA (Language) = (English)). Figure S1, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/P68 showed the inclusion processes used in our study. The English-language articles and reviews most relevant to colchicine for CHD were eligible for subsequent analyses. Our study analyzed publicly available datasets and therefore did not require an ethical statement.

The present systematic review and meta-analysis (CRD420251007309) adhered to the guidelines set forth by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses statement.[11] We systematically searched the PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases for relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating the efficacy of colchicine in CHD patients, covering the period from inception through January 31, 2025, without imposing any language restrictions. We used the following MeSH terms and combined text to guide our search: “colchicine” and “myocardial ischemia.”

sec.title: 2.2. Data collection
sec.p: Two authors (NZ and JW) independently retrieved data and excluded studies irrelevant to the search strategy. All data, including titles, keywords, journals, authors, references, citations, years of publications, institutions, and countries/regions, were extracted from the Web of Science Core Collection database and were eventually included in this manuscript. The newest edition of the Journal Citation Reports (JCR 2023) was used to present the latest impact factors and zoning for each journal.

We included RCTs that evaluated the efficacy of colchicine use in CHD patients. All eligible studies had to report at least one of the predefined clinical endpoints. The primary endpoint was recurrent myocardial infarction, stroke, revascularization, or cardiovascular death. The exclusion criteria were as follows: Individuals under 18 years old; observational and retrospective studies; RCTs that did not report our outcomes of interest; and RCTs that involved cardiopulmonary bypass therapy or used nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Two independent investigators (HW and JW) screened the retrieved studies based on their titles and abstracts. The studies that met the inclusion criteria were then evaluated in full-text form. Two investigators (QC and JZ) extracted data and conducted a comprehensive analysis, while a third investigator (NZ) acted as an arbitrator in cases of disagreement. The quality of the studies was assessed according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses recommendations, and the risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool.

sec.title: 2.3. Data analysis
sec.p: The bibliometric analyses were performed by using VOSviewer (version 1.6.17) and CiteSpace (version 6.1.2). We first employed Excel to visualize the publication and citation trends of colchicine for CHD. The VOSviewer was conducted to show bibliometric networks or density maps of intercountry or organization cooperation, cooccurrence of keywords, and Linkages between journals. The cluster analysis, bursts of keywords, and collaborative networks between authors, institutions, and countries/regions were presented by CiteSpace. The differences in geographical distribution of global publications were visualized by using the Tableau Desktop software.

To assess the clinical benefits of colchicine, we evaluated 4 categorical outcomes. Given the heterogeneity among eligible trials and its potential impact on the observed benefits, we employed the I² statistic to quantify the heterogeneity across trials for each outcome. Significant heterogeneity was defined as a P-value < .1 or an I² value > 50%. In the presence of substantial heterogeneity, we used a random-effects model, based on the restricted maximum likelihood method, to estimate the clinical effects.[12] To assess potential publication bias, we constructed funnel plots for each outcome, provided that the number of included studies exceeded 10. Additionally, we conducted 3 subgroup analyses stratified by the subtype of CHD to explore potential differences in clinical benefits.

sec.title: 3.1. Analysis of the number and trends of publications and citations
sec.p: A total of 94 papers were related to colchicine for CHD from 1996 to 2025 according to the comprehensive screening and were included in the final bibliometric analysis (Figure S1, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/P68 and Appendix 1, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/P68). The overall trend of publication research continued to increase from 2013 onward and peaked in 2021. Then the years 2021 to 2023 were the hot research period (Fig. 1). Additionally, the citation trends showed more significant growth in 2013 to 2020. The rapid growth in the number of publications and citations in recent years suggests that the application of colchicine in the treatment of CHD remains an area of intense scientific focus.

caption.p: The annual number of publications and citations on colchicine for coronary heart disease from 1996 to 2025.

sec.title: 3.2. Analysis of contributions of prolific authors, research teams, and journals
sec.p: The top 10 prolific authors with the highest number of citations in this discipline were listed in Table S1, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/P68. Fiolet ATL from the Netherlands ranked first, with the remainder coming from the Netherlands, Canada, Australia, Athens, and America. Figure 2 showed a collaborative network of authors with the most prolific publications. There were 12 productive research teams on the network visualization graph in Figure 2A. As shown by the overlay graph of the historical trend, 4 new research teams were established and have grown rapidly in recent years (Fig. 2B). Furthermore, the relationship between the distinguished 20 authors, their affiliated institutions, and countries/regions was exhibited in Figure 2C, suggesting that efforts of numerous teams around the world have focused on this anti-inflammatory agent for 22nd-century cardiac patients.

caption.p: Co-authorship analysis of prolific authors and research teams in the field of colchicine for coronary heart disease. (A) A network visualization graph of productive research teams. (B) An overlay visualization graph of the historical trend of productive research teams. (C) Relationship between the top prolific 20 authors, their countries/regions, and affiliated institutions.

sec.p: A dual-map overlay atlas was used to display the distribution of citing and cited journals, where the left and right geographic regions represented citing and cited journals, respectively (Fig. 3). The citing journals were mainly involved in health, nursing, medicine, molecular, biology, and genetics, and the cited journals were mainly concerned with molecular, biology and immunology. Table 1 illustrates the top 10 articles with the highest citation frequencies. The most cited paper entitled ‘Anti-Inflammatory Therapy with Canakinumab for Atherosclerotic Disease’ was published in the NEW ENGL J MED in 2017, which was a milestone in the success of anti-inflammatory therapy for CHD. Furthermore, the paper entitled ‘Low-Dose Colchicine for Secondary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease’ was published in the J AM COLL CARDIOL in 2013, which was the beginning of colchicine’s application to CHD. The density visualization map showed that these 26 references are the most cited (Figure S2, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/P68).

sec.title: 3.3. Analysis of the contributions by institutions and countries
sec.p: The 10 most productive institutions were mainly affiliated with Europe and the United States, as shown in Figure 4A. In addition, we identified 7 clusters of institutions by setting the minimum number of papers published by an institution at 5 (Fig. 4B). The overlay graph of the historical trend showed that a tightly-knit and influential community of authors has emerged in Canadian academic institutions in recent years (Fig. 4C).

Figure 6A displayed the publishing trends of the top 5 nations over time. As shown in Figure 6B and C, we showed the examination of co-authorship among major participating countries and found that Canada, China, Australia, and France have recently engaged in considerable research cooperation.

sec.title: 3.4. Analysis of keywords
sec.p: Figure 7A showed the cluster analysis of all keywords that appeared more than 10 times. High-frequency keywords were divided into 4 clusters according to their relevance. cluster 1 (red cluster): diseases and drug therapy; cluster 2 (green cluster): molecular mechanisms of colchicine; cluster 3 (yellow cluster): network pharmacology; cluster 4 (blue cluster): secondary prevention, nursing and adverse effect monitoring. In Figure 7D, the major keywords with the highest occurrences across the 4 major clusters. Subsequently, we used the timeline picture of high-frequency keywords to show the period and time trend of keyword occurrences (Fig. 7B). The longest-lasting hotspots included interleukin-1β (IL-1β), immunomodulation, and allopurinol, whereas emerging hotspots covered inflammation, cholesterol, and clinical trials. Figure 7C showed the top 25 keywords with the strongest citation bursts to reveal hot research in this field during a specific period.

caption.p: Analysis of keywords. (A) A network visualization map of high-frequency keywords. (B) A timeline and keyword clustering display for the colchicine for coronary heart disease. (C) The top 25 terms with the most significant citation bursts on colchicine for coronary heart disease. (D) Keywords that are particularly important in the 4 clusters.

sec.title: 3.5. Analysis of primary endpoints
sec.p: The initial literature search yielded a total of 336 relevant articles. After applying our predefined eligibility criteria, 12 trials comprising 20,754 participants were deemed suitable for inclusion in the present meta-analysis (Figure S3, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/P68). The risk of bias assessment for this meta-analysis was presented in Figure S4, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/P68. Among them, 4 trials reported on colchicine for stable CHD (SCHD),[5–7,13] and the remaining trials enrolled patients with ACS.[8,13–20]

Colchicine demonstrated significant effects in reducing recurrent myocardial infarction (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.70–0.93; P<0.01), stroke (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.30–0.95; P = .03), and revascularization (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.46–0.95; P = .03), with different degrees of significant between-study heterogeneities (Fig. 8A–C). Despite not achieving statistical significance, colchicine had minimal impacts on cardiovascular death, with no evidence of heterogeneity among the studies (RR 0.96, CI 0.78–1.19; P = .73; Fig. 8D).

caption.p: Forest plots of trials assessing primary endpoints. (A) The effect of colchicine on recurrent myocardial infarction; (B) the effect of colchicine on stroke; (C) the effect of colchicine on revascularization; (D) the effect of colchicine on cardiovascular death.

sec.title: 3.6. Subgroup analyses
sec.p: Subgroup analyses revealed that colchicine demonstrated favorable effects in recurrent myocardial infarction (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.62–0.94; P < .01), stroke (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.19–0.77; P < .01), revascularization (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.44–0.89; P < .01) in patients with SCHD (Fig. 9A–C). However, these benefits were not observed in ACS patients (Fig. 9A–C). Likewise, the clinical benefits of colchicine on cardiovascular death remained problematic (Fig. 9D).

caption.p: Forest plots of trials assessing primary endpoints in subgroups categorized based on the subtype of CHD. (A) The effect of colchicine on recurrent myocardial infarction; (B) the effect of colchicine on stroke; (C) the effect of colchicine on revascularization; (D) the effect of colchicine on cardiovascular death.

sec.title: 4.1. Status and trends in global research
sec.p: According to the analysis of national publication data, the Netherlands and the United States have contributed a significant number of publications. The overall trend of publication research peaked in 2021, and then the years 2021 to 2023 were the hot research period. Canada, China, Australia, and France have engaged in considerable research cooperation during this specific period. From the perspective of the most productive institutions, most of which were affiliated with Europe and the United States. The top 3 institutions were the University of Western Australia, Harvard University, and Virginia Commonwealth University. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that colchicine effectively reduced the incidents of recurrent myocardial infarction, stroke, and revascularization, especially in SCHD patients. Our synergistic and combined application of these 2 methodologies holds promise for greater benefits for CHD patients.

sec.title: 4.2. Analysis of research keywords
sec.p: All keywords with a frequency of higher than 10 by using cluster analysis were divided into 4 major clusters: (1) cluster 1 (red cluster): diseases and drug therapy, (2) cluster 2 (green cluster): the molecular mechanisms of colchicine, (3) cluster 3 (yellow cluster): network pharmacology, and (4) cluster 4 (blue cluster): secondary prevention, nursing and adverse effect monitoring. These clusters can show the main research directions in this field in recent years. By analyzing the timeline picture of high-frequency keywords and the top 25 keywords with the strongest citation bursts, we can observe that colchicine has long been used as a first-line drug for familial Mediterranean fever and gout,[21–23] and keywords related to inflammation, cholesterol, and clinical trials appeared with high frequency from 2015 to 2024, suggesting that clinical trials of colchicine for cardiovascular disease and exploration of potential anti-inflammatory mechanisms of colchicine have gradually become research hotspots.[23] Additionally, clinical indications and precise timing of colchicine use in the CHD populations, as well as secondary prevention, nursing strategies, and adverse effect monitoring, have received increasing attention,[24] which was also consistent with the results of our cluster analysis. Next, we will combine the 4 clusters to explore the research hotspots and directions of colchicine in the treatment of cardiovascular diseases.

sec.title: 4.2.1. Red cluster: diseases and drug therapy
sec.p: The LoDoCo (low-dose colchicine for secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease) trial was the beginning of the use of colchicine in the treatment of cardiovascular disease in recent years.[5] This study, with an average follow-up of 3 years, indicated that colchicine yielded a 67% relative reduction in the composite of ACS, out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, or non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke in individuals with stable coronary disease.[5] Subsequently, the LoDoCo2 (colchicine in patients with chronic coronary disease) trial and the COLCOT (efficacy and safety of low-dose colchicine after myocardial infarction) trial provided more clarity on the benefits of colchicine for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.[6,7] However, there were distinct differences in the type of recruited patients and the timing of drug use between these 2 trials. The LoDoCo2 trial enrolled patients 6 months after the onset of ACS, while the COLCOT trial recruited patients within 30 days after myocardial infarction.[6,7] Selection of SCHD patients for drug administration may account for these clinical benefits. In addition, we performed a detailed analysis of their set outcomes and found that the clinical benefit of the LoDoCo2 trial was driven primarily by a reduction in myocardial infarction, whereas the benefit of the COLCOT trial was derived mainly from a reduction in revascularization and stroke. The Australian COPS randomized clinical trial (colchicine in patients with acute coronary syndrome) recruited ACS patients and added colchicine to guideline-directed medical therapy during hospitalization for 12 months. Unfortunately, colchicine failed to produce cardiovascular benefits and instead was associated with a higher rate of mortality.[8] Furthermore, the second colchicine ACS trial set the duration of colchicine use at 6 months and modified the range of the primary composite endpoint.[17] It was observed that colchicine reduced the risk of predefined endpoint events, mainly due to a reduction in unstable angina.[23] Another clinical trial showed that colchicine was beneficial in preventing restenosis of bare metal stents in diabetic patients with CHD.[25] However, just-released preliminary results from the CLEAR SYNERGY trial demonstrated that the use of colchicine provides little benefit in patients with acute myocardial infarction after percutaneous coronary intervention.[26] Colchicine has been approved by the FDA for the treatment of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease,[10] but the appropriate population, precise timing, and exact benefits of colchicine warrant further evaluation. Of particular interest, although the anti-inflammatory agent colchicine aimed at reducing the risk of residual inflammation in CHD patients, none of the aforementioned landmark colchicine cardiovascular clinical trials required participants to have elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) levels.[23] Even the FDA-approved indications did not mention the need for hs-CRP testing before the administration of colchicine. Varying CRP levels between patient populations may be responsible for yielding different clinical benefits. Therefore, there is a need for large-scale RCTs incorporating CRP levels to recruit patients suitable for colchicine treatment.

Based on the current evidence from available RCTs, we conducted a meta-analysis to summarize the clinical efficacy of colchicine in the treatment of CHD. Our results revealed that colchicine yielded a 20% relative reduction in recurrent myocardial infarction, a 46% relative reduction in stroke, and a 34% relative reduction in revascularization. Nevertheless, significant between-study heterogeneities adequately reflected these differences in study design. Further subgroup analyses demonstrated a novel finding that colchicine showed a promising decline in the primary endpoints among SCHD patients, whereas these benefits were absent in ACS patients. Given the above findings, colchicine may be more suitable for SCHD patients who have high residual inflammatory risk. However, this hypothesis requires further validation through large-scale, multicenter clinical trials to confirm its clinical utility.

sec.title: 4.2.2. Green cluster: molecular mechanisms of colchicine
sec.p: Initially, colchicine was believed to bind to microtubule proteins and suspend cell mitosis, thus applying to the acute phase treatment of gout.[27,28] With continuous improvement in treating CHD, the addition of colchicine to standard medical therapy in patients with ACS significantly improved plaque stability by inhibiting vascular inflammation.[9] Colchicine can lower secretions of IL-1β and IL-18 by directly interfering with the assembly and activation process of NOD-like receptor family, pyrin domain containing 3 inflammation.[28–30] Transcriptomic and Pharmacoproteomic studies indicated that colchicine can regulate the levels of several immune-related proteins, including some circulating neutrophil-related proteins.[31–33] Some experimental studies revealed that colchicine decreased neutrophil chemotaxis and superoxide production.[34,35] Furthermore, colchicine reduced the production of neutrophil extracellular traps to mitigate coronary artery injury and thrombus formation in ACS patients.[35] Additionally, colchicine delivered by a novel nanoparticle platform selectively the NF-κB signaling pathway in endothelial cells and macrophages in animal models.[36–38] However, which molecules directly bind to colchicine to exert anti-inflammatory effects remains an active area of investigation. Colchicine can also reduce the uptake of cholesterol crystals and inhibit foam cell formation by downregulating the expression of CD36.[39] These provided new insights into the role of colchicine in anti-atherosclerosis and plaque stabilization.

sec.title: 4.2.3. Yellow cluster: network pharmacology
sec.p: Network pharmacology is an emerging systems biology methodology that aims to elucidate the mechanisms of action and poly-pharmacological effects of drugs by constructing and analyzing complex biomolecular networks. This approach transcends the limitations of traditional single-target drug research by highlighting the intricate, multi-dimensional interactions between drugs and biological systems. As a result, network pharmacology offers a more comprehensive understanding of the holistic effects and potential side effects of medications, providing a deeper insight into their therapeutic profiles. Currently, there is a paucity of research utilizing network pharmacology to explore the mechanisms of action of colchicine. A previous investigation indicated that colchicine potentially exerted its therapeutic effects on CHD by targeting proteins such as Cytochrome c, Myeloperoxidase, and Histone deacetylase 1.[40] The proposed mechanism of action is likely associated with the cellular response to chemical stimuli and the p75NTR-mediated negative regulation of the cell cycle by SC1.[40] Likewise, it has been demonstrated that colchicine can prevent H9C2 cell apoptosis triggered by myocardial ischemia–reperfusion injury through the activation of the PI3K/AKT/eNOS signaling cascade.[41] Nevertheless, research exploring the mechanisms of action of colchicine through network pharmacology is still relatively scarce. Hence, innovative research approaches hold significant potential for elucidating the mechanisms underlying colchicine in the treatment of CHD.

sec.title: 4.2.4. Blue cluster: secondary prevention, nursing, and adverse effect monitoring
sec.p: While colchicine has received FDA approval as a complementary treatment to standard medical therapy for cardiovascular diseases, it has yet to be incorporated into the secondary prevention protocols for CHD in China. Thus, Chinese medical professionals possess comparatively limited experience in the clinical application of colchicine for the treatment of CHD. In recent years, our study found that China, Canada, Australia, and France have engaged in considerable research collaboration by analyzing the participation of countries and regions in the global distribution of publications. There were no differences in severe and infrequent adverse reactions associated with colchicine, including leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and neuropathy, when compared between the colchicine and placebo groups in both the COLCOT and LoDoCo2 trials.[6,7] Similar to its use in treating gout, the COLOTO study found that colchicine administration in CHD patients increased the risk of gastrointestinal events by 74%.[6,42] However, this medication-induced diarrhea was self-limiting and often resolved within 3 days in many cases. Employing a lower dose of colchicine seems to be an effective approach to alleviating this issue.[43] Individuals who received colchicine exhibited a notably higher rate of pneumonia in the COLCOT trial.[6] In contrast, systematic reviews and meta-analyses have failed to uncover any significant differences in infectious outcomes between colchicine and placebo.[4,42] This matter warrants additional investigation and confirmation through a multicenter collaboration with researchers from different countries.

Colchicine undergoes hepatic metabolism via the cytochrome P450 3A4 enzyme, which can lead to drug-drug interactions and exacerbate adverse effects.[23] For example, concurrent use of statins with colchicine may increase the potential risk of severe liver injury, myalgia, or myotoxicity.[24,44] It is more appropriate for patients with CHD to choose rosuvastatin, which is not a cytochrome P450 3A4 substrate, when co-administered with colchicine.[44,45] Regarding antiarrhythmic medications, it is advisable to circumvent the combination of colchicine with diltiazem or verapamil whenever possible.[44] It is imperative to collaborate with electrophysiologists and experienced nursing staff to evaluate and monitor for potential adverse reactions before the use of colchicine.[42,44] Therefore, drug-drug interactions pose a formidable clinical challenge for nursing care and surveillance of adverse effects. Exploring the interactions between colchicine and other medications will offer a safeguard in clinical practice.

sec.title: 4.3. Limitations
sec.p: This study faced several limitations. Firstly, our study included only English-language literature, potentially leading to selection bias by excluding meaningful research published in other languages. Secondly, the latest high-quality articles may not have been included in this bibliometric analysis due to their short period since publication and limited citation rates. Thirdly, due to the unavailability of individual participant data, we were unable to conduct a direct comparison of the efficacy of colchicine in different subtypes of CHD within our analysis.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: This study offers a thorough quantitative and qualitative evaluation of studies about colchicine in the treatment of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Over the past decades, there has been a significant surge in the number of publications in this field. We have established 4 future research hotspots by analyzing the keywords with the strongest citation bursts. Notably, research into the therapeutic indications and Molecular Mechanisms of colchicine in treating CHD has become an area of intense scientific focus. The appropriate indication for colchicine therapy should be patients with SCHD who have high residual inflammatory risk.
